# Docling Document Chatbot

An offline document chatbot that converts HTML documents into Markdown using Docling and answers questions using a local Qwen 2.5 1.5B model through llama.cpp.

The initial example document contains BGP and MRT technical information. The input HTML can be replaced with another document without changing the chatbot backend.

An offline document chatbot that converts HTML documents into Markdown using Docling and answers questions using a local Qwen 2.5 1.5B model through llama.cpp.

section: Docling Document Chatbot > 1. Architecture
text:
## 1. Architecture

The application has four main components:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Docling | Converts the input HTML document into Markdown |
| Markdown document | Stores the extracted document content |
| Qwen 2.5 1.5B | Generates answers using the local language model |
| llama.cpp | Runs the Qwen model locally and provides an API |
| Flask backend | Reads the Markdown document and handles chatbot requests |
| ChromaDB | Stores verified exact-question and answer cache entries |
| LibreChat | Provides the chat interface |

section: Docling Document Chatbot > 1. Architecture > Workflow
text:
### Workflow

1. The user provides an HTML document.
2. Docling converts the HTML into `output.md`.
3. The Flask backend reads the generated Markdown file.
4. The backend sends the document context and question to the local Qwen model through llama.cpp.
5. The answer is returned through the backend.
6. LibreChat provides the user interface.

The chatbot is designed to answer using the supplied document. If the document does not contain the requested information, the backend returns:

```text
The document does not contain this information.
```

ChromaDB is used only for verified exact-question answer caching. It is not used for document retrieval or similarity-based search.

cd docling-chatbot

```bash

source venv/bin/activate

- `Flask` – chatbot backend
- `chromadb` – verified-answer cache

section: Docling Document Chatbot > 5. Install and build llama.cpp
text:
## 5. Install and build llama.cpp

llama.cpp runs the local GGUF language model and provides the API used by the chatbot backend.

Install the build tools:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git cmake build-essential
```

Clone llama.cpp:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git
```

Build it:

```bash
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build --config Release -j2
```

Check that the server executable exists:

```bash
ls -lh build/bin/llama-server
```

Return to the chatbot project directory:

```bash
cd ..
```

text:
## 6. Download the Qwen model

The chatbot uses:

- Model: Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct
- Format: GGUF
- Quantization: Q4_K_M

Create the model directory:

```bash
mkdir -p models
```

Download the model:

```bash
wget -O models/qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf \
"https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/main/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf"
```

Check the downloaded file:

```bash
ls -lh models/
```

The model is approximately 1 GB. It is not included in this repository and must be downloaded separately.

section: Docling Document Chatbot > 7. Convert HTML into Markdown
text:
## 7. Convert HTML into Markdown

The initial input document is:

```text
input.html
```

The conversion script is `main.py`.

It uses Docling to:

1. Read the HTML document.
2. Extract and structure its content.
3. Export the extracted content into Markdown.
4. Save the result as `output.md`.

Run the conversion from the project directory:

```bash
python main.py
```

Check the generated file:

```bash
ls -lh output.md
```

To inspect the generated Markdown:

```bash
less output.md
```

The backend requires `output.md`, so complete this conversion before starting the chatbot backend.

text:
## 8. Start the llama.cpp server

Open a separate terminal.

Navigate to the project directory:

```bash
cd docling-chatbot
```

Start the local model server:

```bash
./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
-m ./models/qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf \
--host 127.0.0.1 \
--port 8080 \
-c 4096 \
-t 2
```

The server listens at:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

Keep this terminal running while using the chatbot.

Create `librechat.yaml` in the LibreChat directory:

```yaml
version: 1.3.18

cache: true

endpoints:
  custom:
    - name: "DocumentBot"
      apiKey: "local-no-key"
      baseURL: "http://host.docker.internal:5001/v1"
      models:
        default:
          - "local-model"
        fetch: false
      titleConvo: false
      modelDisplayLabel: "Document Chatbot"
```

section: Docling Document Chatbot > 12. Use another HTML document
text:
## 12. Use another HTML document

The chatbot can be used with another HTML document.

1. Keep a copy of the original `input.html`.
2. Replace the contents of `input.html` with the new HTML document.
3. Keep the filename as `input.html`.
4. Run the conversion again:

```bash
   python main.py
   ```

5. Confirm that the new `output.md` has been generated.
6. Restart the backend if it is already running.
7. Ask questions about the new document.

The conversion script currently expects the filename `input.html`. The backend expects the generated filename `output.md`.

The Python backend does not need to be rewritten just to change the document.

section: FRR MRT Lab
text:
# FRR MRT Lab

Two-router eBGP labs that write MRT dumps (`updates`, `updates-tx`, `routes-mrt`)
to the host. There are two independent labs — **operator 1** and **operator 2** —
and two ways to run each: **containerlab** or **docker compose**.

| | Operator 1 | Operator 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Routers | `op1r1` (AS 64512) ↔ `op1r2` (AS 64513) | `op2r1` (AS 64515) ↔ `op2r2` (AS 64516) |
| Peering link | `192.168.100.1/29` ↔ `192.168.100.2/29` | `192.200.100.1/29` ↔ `192.200.100.2/29` |
| Advertised prefix | `10.10.0.0/24` (from `op1r1`) | `20.20.0.0/24` (from `op2r1`) |
| Configs | `configs-operator-1/` | `configs-operator-2/` |
| MRT output | `operator1_mrt/` | `operator2_mrt/` |

Both run-methods use the **same** config files, so pick whichever you prefer.

# FRR MRT Lab

Two-router eBGP labs that write MRT dumps (`updates`, `updates-tx`, `routes-mrt`)
to the host. There are two independent labs — **operator 1** and **operator 2** —
and two ways to run each: **containerlab** or **docker compose**.

| | Operator 1 | Operator 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Routers | `op1r1` (AS 64512) ↔ `op1r2` (AS 64513) | `op2r1` (AS 64515) ↔ `op2r2` (AS 64516) |
| Peering link | `192.168.100.1/29` ↔ `192.168.100.2/29` | `192.200.100.1/29` ↔ `192.200.100.2/29` |
| Advertised prefix | `10.10.0.0/24` (from `op1r1`) | `20.20.0.0/24` (from `op2r1`) |
| Configs | `configs-operator-1/` | `configs-operator-2/` |
| MRT output | `operator1_mrt/` | `operator2_mrt/` |

Both run-methods use the **same** config files, so pick whichever you prefer.

## 1. Build the image

Both labs need one image: `frr-local:mrt-tx` — upstream FRR at a pinned commit
plus `frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff`, the `dump bgp updates-tx` patch carried in this
directory. Everything needed is in this repository:

```sh
cd frr-mrt

git clone git@github.com:FRRouting/frr.git
cd frr
git checkout d5a6ba7e0cae53f8ea65b98c470cf26f9dd077a4
patch -p1 < ../frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff

docker build \
    --file=docker/alpine/Dockerfile \
    --build-arg=PKGVER=0 \
    --tag=frr-local:mrt-tx \
    .
```

~10–15 min cold, a couple of minutes cached.

Check it:

```sh
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh frr-local:mrt-tx -c '/usr/lib/frr/bgpd --version | head -1'

section: bgpd version 10.8.0-dev_git0 > Notes on the build
text:
### Notes on the build

- **The pinned commit is not optional.** The patch touches `bgpd/bgp_dump.c`,
  `bgpd/bgp_packet.c`, `docker/alpine/Dockerfile`, `doc/user/bgp.rst` and one
  topotest. It is generated against `d5a6ba7e` and will not apply cleanly to a
  moving `master`.
- **Clone inside `frr-mrt/`**, as above — that is what makes the relative
  `../frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff` resolve. The `frr-mrt/frr/` clone is gitignored, so
  it will not show up as an untracked nested repository.
- **The build reads the working tree** (`COPY . /src`), so the patch does not
  need to be committed in the clone. `git apply ../frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff` works
  in place of `patch -p1` if you prefer.
- **A prebuilt image is planned** so this build is not needed on every host. It
  is not published yet — build from source for now.

## 4. Generate updates

Flap the advertised route on `op2r1` — withdraw it, then put it back. Each step
produces a real BGP UPDATE that lands in the MRT dumps.

Drop into the shell:

```sh
docker exec -it clab-bgp-operator2_mrt-op2r1 vtysh
```

Withdraw:

```
op2r1# conf t
op2r1(config)# no ip route 20.20.0.0/24 Null0
op2r1(config)# exit
```

Re-advertise:

```
op2r1# conf t
op2r1(config)# ip route 20.20.0.0/24 Null0
op2r1(config)# exit

```sh
docker exec clab-bgp-operator2_mrt-op2r1 vtysh -c 'conf t' -c 'no ip route 20.20.0.0/24 Null0'

section: op2r1-rib-20260829-0649.mrt            table dump > Gotchas
text:
## Gotchas

- **`pull access denied for frr-local`** — the image isn't built. Run step 1. Both
  topologies reference `frr-local:mrt-tx`; docker only tries the registry when
  the tag is missing locally.
- **Peering links are `/29`, not `/30`.** Docker compose needs room for a gateway
  address in the subnet, which a `/30` has no space for. The `/29` keeps a single
  set of config files working under both launch methods.
- **Operator 1 compose vs. `mrt-tx-net`** — a leftover `docker network`
  (`192.168.100.0/24`) overlaps operator 1's peering subnet and compose will
  refuse to create it. Remove it if unused: `docker network rm mrt-tx-net`.
- **`Node name will not resolve via DNS`** — the `_` in the containerlab topology
  name `bgp-operator2_mrt`. Cosmetic; the lab works.
- **`Can't open configuration file /etc/frr/vtysh.conf`** — harmless, the image
  ships no `vtysh.conf`.
- **MRT bind dirs must stay world-writable** (`operator1_mrt/`, `operator2_mrt/`)
  — `frr` is uid 100 inside the image.
- **`sudo` and containerlab** — if your user is in `clab_admins` and the `docker`
  group, `clab deploy` works without `sudo`. Mixing the two leaves lab
  directories owned by different users, so pick one and stay with it.

## Appendix: compile-only check

Faster loop when you only want to know whether the tree builds — no runtime image.

```sh
cd /home/yogesh/frr-mrt-lab/frr

docker build \
    --file=docker/alpine/Dockerfile \
    --build-arg=PKGVER=0 \
    --tag=frr-src:mrt-tx \
    --target=source-builder \
    .

docker run --rm frr-src:mrt-tx sh -c 'cd /src && make -j"$(nproc)" bgpd/bgpd'
```

Note: `bgpd -C` on a config containing a `router bgp` stanza aborts during
teardown with `bgp_keepalives_off(): assertion (fpt->running) failed`. That is
pre-existing on master, not an MRT regression — the config has already parsed by
then, so a non-zero rc there is not a parse failure.

Cleanup — these build images are ~1.7 GB:

```sh
docker image rm frr-src:mrt-tx frr-built:mrt-tx
docker builder prune -f
```

text:
#### 1. `frr-local:mrt-tx` — the operator routers

FRR with the `dump bgp updates-tx` extension: upstream FRR at a pinned commit,
plus [`frr-mrt/frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff`](../../frr-mrt/frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff),
which is carried in this repository. Full notes: `frr-mrt/README.md` step 1.

```sh
cd multi-mrt-data-poc/tenancy
make frr-image        # or `make frr` — same target
```

That runs [`frr-mrt/prepare-frr-mrt-image.sh`](../../frr-mrt/prepare-frr-mrt-image.sh),
which clones upstream FRR into `frr-mrt/frr`, pins the commit, applies the patch,
builds the image and prints the `bgpd` version.

**This is a one-time, per-host step — deliberately outside `make all`.** It takes
~10-15 min cold and the image is then reused by every lab run, so it is not part
of the routine pipeline. Re-running it is cheap and safe: an existing
`frr-local:mrt-tx` is detected and the build skipped (`FORCE=1 make frr-image`
rebuilds anyway). The script is re-runnable from any directory, reuses an
existing clone, and resets the tree before patching, so a half-finished earlier
attempt does not need cleaning up first.

By hand, if you would rather not use the target:

```sh
cd frr-mrt
git clone https://github.com/FRRouting/frr.git
cd frr
git checkout d5a6ba7e0cae53f8ea65b98c470cf26f9dd077a4
git apply ../frr-bgp-mrt-v0.1.diff
docker build --file=docker/alpine/Dockerfile --build-arg=PKGVER=0 \
             --tag=frr-local:mrt-tx .
```

Check it:

```sh
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh frr-local:mrt-tx \
  -c '/usr/lib/frr/bgpd --version | head -1'

## 3. Start the operator labs

Two independent two-router eBGP labs write MRT to `frr-mrt/operator{1,2}_mrt/`.

```sh
make labs        # or, by hand:
cd frr-mrt
clab deploy -t bgp-mrt.operator1.clab.yml
clab deploy -t bgp-mrt.operator2.clab.yml
```

**Use containerlab, not docker compose.** Both launch methods work, but compose
needs a docker network on the operator-1 peering subnet, and a leftover
`mrt-tx-net` (`192.168.100.0/24`) commonly collides with it. Containerlab wires
the link as a direct veth pair and sidesteps the conflict entirely.

Confirm the sessions are up — you want a **number** under `State/PfxRcd`, not
`Active` or `Connect`:

```sh
docker exec clab-bgp-mrt-op1r1 vtysh -c 'show ip bgp summary'
docker exec clab-bgp-operator2_mrt-op2r1 vtysh -c 'show ip bgp summary'
```

### What the labs advertise

| Tenant | Originating router | Prefixes | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| operator1 | `op1r1` — **AS 12654** | `84.205.66.0/24` | public origin is 12654 → `ORIGIN_MATCH` |
| | | `187.249.2.0/24` | public origin is 32098 → `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` |
| | | `10.10.0.0/24` | absent from public data → `NOT_OBSERVED_GLOBALLY` |
| operator2 | `op2r1` — AS 64515 | `20.20.0.0/24` | private space; stays unobserved |

Operator 1 runs a real ASN and real prefixes **so that each twin validation
outcome actually fires** against real public data. The lab is sealed — two
containers on a veth pair, no external peering — so nothing is announced
anywhere. See `frr-mrt/configs-operator-1/op1r1.conf`.

text:
## 4. Generate MRT to ingest

A freshly deployed lab converges once and then goes quiet: RIB files rotate, but
`updates`/`updates-tx` stay zero-byte because nothing changes. **Without this
step there is no update data at all** — the exact state operator 1 was found in.

```sh
make labdata                                    # 3 cycles, both tenants, ~2.5 min
python3 app/labdata.py --tenant operator1 --cycles 5   # or target one tenant
```

It withdraws and re-announces each tenant's prefixes on its originating router,
spacing flaps so they land in more than one 1-minute rotation. Routers,
containers and prefixes all come from `config/tenants.yaml`.

text:
## 5. Run the pipeline

`make all` runs everything. To go stage by stage:

| Command | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `make census` | Decodes every MRT file and reports per-kind counts. Asserts that `size > 0` and "decodes to ≥1 element" agree. | ~2 min |
| `make extract` | MRT → tenant-tagged Parquet, one directory per tenant. | ~1 min |
| `make replay` | Route state + change log + advertised routes, per tenant. | **~10 min** |
| `make views` | Per-tenant merged views (`public ∪ own`) and twin views. | seconds |
| `make up` | Starts per-tenant Neo4j and per-tenant API processes. | ~1 min |
| `make graph` | Loads each tenant's own graph. | ~1 min |
| `make test` | Contract + isolation assertions. | ~1 min |

`make replay` dominates: replay is row-by-row, so the 50,000-element public
sample takes about ten minutes. The operators' own data replays in seconds — if
you only changed lab data, re-run just that tenant and skip the public pass:

```sh
python3 app/extract.py --tenant operator1
python3 app/replay.py  --tenant operator1
make views && make graph
```

### The twin queries

```sh
python3 - <<'EOF'
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect('work/views/operator1/view.duckdb', read_only=True)
for r in con.execute("""
    SELECT prefix, advertised_origin, observed_origin, observing_peers, outcome
    FROM twin_origin_validation ORDER BY outcome""").fetchall():
    print(r)
EOF
```

Expect all three outcomes:

```
('10.10.0.0/24',   12654,  None, None, 'NOT_OBSERVED_GLOBALLY')
('84.205.66.0/24', 12654, 12654,   34, 'ORIGIN_MATCH')
('187.249.2.0/24', 12654, 32098,   20, 'ORIGIN_MISMATCH')
```

AS 12654; twenty say `187.249.2.0/24` originates in AS 32098, contradicting the
operator and firing `twin_possible_hijack`.

Other views in the same database: `twin_advertised`, `twin_possible_hijack`,
`twin_not_propagated`, `twin_multi_origin`, `twin_my_peers`,
`twin_global_view_of_me`.

text:
### Connecting from another machine

The published ports bind to `0.0.0.0`, so they are reachable over the network
already — swap `localhost` for the host's LAN IP.

**Neo4j Browser defaults to the `neo4j://` scheme, and that needs one setting.**
`neo4j://` performs routing discovery: the server hands the *client* an address
to connect back on, taken from `server.bolt.advertised_address`. Neo4j's default
is `localhost:7687`, which tells a remote laptop to connect to **itself** — the
symptom is:

```
ServiceUnavailable: Could not perform discovery. No routing servers available.
Known routing table: RoutingTable[... routers=[], readers=[], writers=[]]
```

Two ways out, and you can use either:

1. **Use `bolt://` instead**, which skips discovery entirely and needs no server
   change. In the Neo4j Browser connect dialog, set the URL to
   `bolt://<host-ip>:7688`.
2. **Advertise a reachable address**, so `neo4j://` works too. Set
   `ATLAS_ADVERTISED_HOST` in [`.env`](.env) to the host's LAN IP and restart:

```sh
   echo 'ATLAS_ADVERTISED_HOST=10.0.0.5' > .env   # your host's IP
   docker compose up -d
   ```

Confirm the server now hands out the right address:

```sh
   docker exec atlas-neo4j-operator1 cypher-shell -u neo4j -p operator1pass \
     "CALL dbms.routing.getRoutingTable({}, 'neo4j') YIELD servers RETURN servers;"
   ```

The published port (7688/7689) must appear, not the in-container 7687.

The tenant APIs reach Neo4j over the compose network with `bolt://`, so they
never consult the routing table and are unaffected by this setting.

If a port is unreachable from the laptop, it is a network issue, not a config
one — check `nc -zv <host-ip> 7688`, then the host firewall
(`sudo ufw status`).

text:
### Over an SSH tunnel

A tunnel avoids firewall changes entirely. Forward one port per service you
want, including a Bolt port per tenant:

```sh
ssh -N -L 7475:localhost:7475 -L 7688:localhost:7688 \
       -L 7476:localhost:7476 -L 7689:localhost:7689 \
       -L 12351:localhost:12351 -L 12352:localhost:12352 user@<host-ip>
```

**Use `bolt://` over a tunnel — `neo4j://` cannot work.** The two fixes above
pull in opposite directions: setting `ATLAS_ADVERTISED_HOST` to the LAN IP is
what makes `neo4j://` work for a *direct* client, and it is exactly what breaks
it through a tunnel, because the tunnel maps only `localhost` and the client is
handed the LAN IP instead. `bolt://` ignores the advertised address, so it is
the one form that works in **both** setups — prefer it always.

In Neo4j Browser, note that two defaults are wrong for a tunnel: the scheme
(`neo4j://`) and the port (`7687`, which is not forwarded). Set the Connect URL
to `bolt://localhost:7688` for operator1, `bolt://localhost:7689` for operator2.

| Setup | `bolt://` | `neo4j://` |
|---|---|---|
| Direct to LAN IP, `ATLAS_ADVERTISED_HOST` set | works | works |
| Direct to LAN IP, advertised left as `localhost` | works | fails — discovery returns `localhost` |
| SSH tunnel | works | fails — discovery returns the LAN IP |

> **These services have no meaningful access control.** Neo4j uses placeholder
> passwords from `compose.yaml`, and the tenant APIs have **no authentication at
> all** — anyone who can reach `<host>:12351` gets operator1's full merged view.
> On an untrusted network prefer the SSH tunnel, and bind the published ports to
> loopback by changing `"7688:7687"` to `"127.0.0.1:7688:7687"` in
> `compose.yaml`.

text:
## 9. Troubleshooting

**`Conflicting lock is held` from DuckDB** — a previous run left a process
holding the state database. `pkill -f app/replay.py`, then re-run. DuckDB takes
an exclusive lock: while a writer holds it, even read-only opens fail.

**`pull access denied for frr-local`** — the FRR image was never built. Run
`make frr-image` (section 2, step 1).

**Census reports zero files** — the operator directory is empty, or the labs
were never deployed. Check `docker ps` for `clab-bgp-*` containers.

**`updates`/`updates-tx` all zero-byte** — the lab converged and went quiet. Run
`make labdata` (section 4).

**`Can't open configuration file /etc/frr/vtysh.conf`** — harmless. The FRR image
ships no `vtysh.conf`; the command still applied.

**`Node name will not resolve via DNS`** — cosmetic, from the `_` in the
operator-2 topology name.

**API returns `converting NULL to int64 is unsupported`** — the extract step ran
without origin derivation. Re-run `make extract` and `make replay`; locally
originated RIB entries need `origin_derived`.

**A twin prefix unexpectedly reports `NOT_OBSERVED_GLOBALLY`** — check whether it
is a *routing beacon*. Beacons announce and withdraw on a schedule and may end
the sample withdrawn, so they are legitimately absent from current route state.
`84.205.80.0/24` behaves this way; `84.205.66.0/24` does not.

**Ports already in use** — 7475/7476, 7688/7689, 12351/12352. Note the reference
`internet-mapper-api` stack uses 7474/7687/12345 and can run alongside. Because
both stacks are up at once, a driver pointed at `localhost:7687` reaches the
**reference** database, not a tenant's — check the prefix count (a tenant graph
has thousands; the reference sample has one) if results look wrong.

**`Could not perform discovery. No routing servers available.`** — a remote
client used `neo4j://` and was handed an address it cannot reach: `localhost`
when connecting directly, or the LAN IP when connecting through a tunnel. Switch
the Connect URL to `bolt://…`, which skips discovery. See §7, "Connecting from
another machine".

## Step 2 — operator2's graph *(second browser tab)*

Open **http://localhost:7476/browser/** — note **7476**, not 7475 — and connect
with `bolt://localhost:7689`, `neo4j` / `operator2pass`.

Keep both tabs open. Run [`02-operator2-browser.cypher`](02-operator2-browser.cypher)
query **2.3** next to operator1's **1.3**:

| Query | operator1 sees | operator2 sees |
|---|---|---|
| Who originates `187.249.2.0/24`? | AS 12654 *(private)* **and** AS 32098 *(public)* | AS 32098 *(public)* **only** |

Same prefix, same question, two tenants, different answers. operator1's claim
about its own network is invisible to operator2 — while the public half is
identical for both.

Then **2.4** and **2.5** together make the security model precise:

- `10.10.0.0/24` → **0 nodes.** operator1 never propagated it, so it exists only
  in operator1's own data, and operator2 has no path to it.
- `84.205.66.0/24` → **visible, scope `public`.** Not a leak. It is in the global
  routing table, so every tenant sees it. What operator2 cannot see is
  operator1's *own observation* of it — which is why the scope reads `public`
  here and `both` in operator1's graph.

> **The rule, in one line:** an operator's prefixes are public knowledge; its
> *view* of them is not.

Keep both tabs open. Run [`02-operator2-browser.cypher`](02-operator2-browser.cypher)
query **2.3** next to operator1's **1.3**:

| Query | operator1 sees | operator2 sees |
|---|---|---|
| Who originates `187.249.2.0/24`? | AS 12654 *(private)* **and** AS 32098 *(public)* | AS 32098 *(public)* **only** |

Same prefix, same question, two tenants, different answers. operator1's claim
about its own network is invisible to operator2 — while the public half is
identical for both.

Then **2.4** and **2.5** together make the security model precise:

- `10.10.0.0/24` → **0 nodes.** operator1 never propagated it, so it exists only
  in operator1's own data, and operator2 has no path to it.
- `84.205.66.0/24` → **visible, scope `public`.** Not a leak. It is in the global
  routing table, so every tenant sees it. What operator2 cannot see is
  operator1's *own observation* of it — which is why the scope reads `public`
  here and `both` in operator1's graph.

> **The rule, in one line:** an operator's prefixes are public knowledge; its
> *view* of them is not.

text:
## What to say about honesty

Two caveats belong in the telling, not the footnotes:

**The lab is sealed and the scenario is deliberate.** operator1 was configured to
announce `187.249.2.0/24` so the mismatch fires. Two containers on a virtual
link, no external peering — nothing is announced anywhere. This proves the
*detection logic is correct*; it is not evidence anyone is hijacking that prefix.
The public half of every comparison is genuine RouteViews data.

**There is no authentication.** The tenants are separated by port number. Ports
are not a security boundary. The isolation being demonstrated is of *data paths*
— separate files, separate database processes, separate API processes — not of
*access control*, which is the first thing to build before this faces a real
tenant.

# End-to-end demo

Everything below documents the PoCs individually, each with its own compose file
and hand-copied inputs. To run the **whole chain as one thing** — MRT → parquet
→ route state → Neo4j → API → browser UI — use `internet-mapper-api`, which
orchestrates these same PoC directories with a shared `work/` handoff directory
and no `cp` steps:

```bash
cd internet-mapper-api
make demo                        # fetch, build, ingest, serve, walk every endpoint
open http://localhost:12345/ui/
```

See [internet-mapper-api/README.md](internet-mapper-api/README.md). It replaces
`graph/graph-compose.yaml` (see [graph/README.md](graph/README.md)); the two
cannot run at once because both publish Neo4j on 7474/7687.

The sections below remain the reference for running each stage on its own.

# internet-mapper-api — end-to-end PoC

One compose project that runs the whole chain: MRT dump → parquet → route state
→ Neo4j graph → HTTP API → browser UI. The individual PoCs are unchanged; this
directory orchestrates them and adds the serving layer.

```
                 ┌── stage1-mrt-decode  (../mrt-decode, Rust)
                 │      work/parsed_mrt.txt
                 ├── stage2-parquet     (../converter-parquet, pyarrow)
                 │      work/bgp_updates.parquet
                 ├── stage3-route-state (../route-state/app, DuckDB)
   MRT dump ─────┤      work/current_route_state.parquet + work/change_log.parquet
                 ├── stage4-as-graph    (../graph-poc/loader)
                 │      neo4j: (:AutonomousSystem)-[:ADJACENT_TO]->(:AutonomousSystem)
                 ├── stage5-prefix-graph (../prefix-graph/loader)
                 │      neo4j: (:AutonomousSystem)-[:ORIGINATES|SEEN_VIA]->(:Prefix)
                 └── stage6-enrich      (../enrich-graph/loader, live fetch)

                               + PeeringDB name/org/country on :AutonomousSystem
                                        │

                                            Neo4j over Bolt
```

Every stage shares `./work` as its handoff directory, so **nothing is copied
between PoC folders by hand**. `work/` is regenerated by the pipeline and
gitignored; it holds no source.

section: internet-mapper-api — end-to-end PoC > Run it
text:
## Run it

```bash
make demo        # fetch + build + pipeline + up + walk every endpoint
```

That is the whole demo. It is idempotent — rerun it any time. Step by step:

```bash
make fetch       # download the sample MRT (skipped if ../mrt-decode/data/updates.gz exists)
make build       # api image + the five stage images
make pipeline    # stages 1-5, in order, each failing loudly
make up          # neo4j + api, waits for /health
make smoke       # assert every endpoint answers (and that 404s stay 404s)
make queries     # the cypher packs from graph-poc + prefix-graph
open http://localhost:12345/ui/
```

Individual stages: `make stage1` … `make stage6`. Teardown: `make clean`
(containers) or `make nuke` (containers, volumes, and `work/`).

Stage 6 enriches the graph from **CAIDA AS-relationships** and **PeeringDB**. It
adds no nodes: it tags `:ADJACENT_TO` edges with a CAIDA `relationship_type`
(`p2c`/`p2p`) + `relationship_source`, and sets PeeringDB `name`, `organization`,
`country` and network classification on `:AutonomousSystem` nodes. It only keeps
external records that touch ASNs already in the graph, and is idempotent, so a
small MRT sample yields only a handful of matches — a bigger sample enriches
more. Surface it at `GET /api/v1/asn/{asn}` (identity) and on
`GET /api/v1/asn/{asn}/neighbors` (relationship per pair).

Like the MRT sample, the raw source files are **cached locally** in
`./enrich-graph/input` (the CAIDA `*.as-rel2.txt.bz2` and PeeringDB
`peeringdb_net.json` / `peeringdb_org.json`). The stage reaches the network only
on the first run or when a cached file is missing; every rerun reads the local
copies, so it is fast and works offline once populated. Force a fresh download
with `FORCE_REFRESH=true make stage6`, or clear the cache by deleting those
files. Skip a source entirely with `SKIP_CAIDA=true SKIP_PEERINGDB=true make
stage6` (e.g. offline with no cache yet). `make nuke` leaves the cache in place,
same as it does for the MRT sample.

text:
If the stage-6 **container** has no outbound network (some sandboxes block it),
pre-seed the cache from the host with **`make fetch-enrich`** — the same
download-if-missing pattern as `make fetch`, but for CAIDA + PeeringDB. It is a
prerequisite of `make demo`, so the default flow works with or without container
egress.

Budget **~12 minutes** for a clean `make demo` on a busy machine — most of it is
the Rust and cgo image builds plus two cold Neo4j starts. Reruns are far
quicker.

If a run is interrupted (Ctrl-C, closed terminal), `docker compose run` leaves
its stage container alive, and a live stage 3 keeps the route-state DuckDB file
locked. The next run then fails with
`Could not set lock on file "/state/route_state.db": Conflicting lock is held in
PID 0` — DuckDB says PID 0 because the holder lives in another PID namespace.
`make guard` (a prerequisite of every stage) catches this and tells you to run:

```bash
make unlock      # clear stage containers left behind by an interrupted run
```

text:
### Knobs

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `MRT_LIMIT` | `100` | records parsed from the MRT dump |
| `MRT_SOURCE` | `/mrt/updates.gz` | local path **or** an https URL — the Rust parser takes either |
| `COLLECTOR` | `route-views4` | collector name stamped into the parquet |
| `RESET_STATE` | `false` | `true` discards the incremental route-state DB first |
| `MRT_URL` | RIPE rrc00 2026-01-31 23:00 | what `make fetch` downloads |
| `FORCE_REFRESH` | `false` | `true` re-downloads stage 6 sources even if cached in `enrich-graph/input` |
| `CAIDA_FILE_URL` | *(auto)* | pin a specific serial-2 file; empty auto-discovers the newest |
| `PEERINGDB_API_KEY` | *(none)* | optional PeeringDB API key for higher rate limits |
| `SKIP_CAIDA` / `SKIP_PEERINGDB` | `false` | skip one source in stage 6 (e.g. when offline) |

`make pipeline` is incremental by design: stage 3 keeps its DuckDB state in a
named volume and skips events it has already processed, so a second pass over
the same input produces no new changes. Use `make reset-pipeline` for a clean
single pass — that is what makes `change_log.parquet` reflect exactly one run.

A bigger sample gives a much better demo (multi-origin prefixes and origin
changes are rare in 100 records):

```bash
MRT_LIMIT=50000 make reset-pipeline && make reload
```

text:
## Endpoints

`GET /openapi.yaml` is the full spec; `GET /ui/` is the bundled explorer.
Prefixes are URL-encoded in paths (`8.8.8.0%2F24`).

| Endpoint | Store |
|---|---|
| `/health` | both, plus which parquet files are bound |
| `/api/v1/stats`, `/api/v1/snapshot` | DuckDB + Neo4j counts |
| `/api/v1/examples` | a prefix and ASN that exist in the loaded data |
| `/api/v1/prefix/{p}` | DuckDB summary **joined with** Neo4j origins |
| `/api/v1/prefix/{p}/paths`, `/history` | DuckDB |
| `/api/v1/asn/{asn}/neighbors`, `/prefixes` | Neo4j |
| `/api/v1/graph/neighborhood/{asn}` | Neo4j — `{nodes, edges}` for rendering |
| `/api/v1/analytics/top-origins`, `/collectors`, `/unstable-prefixes` | DuckDB |
| `/api/v1/analytics/hotspots` | **DuckDB churn × Neo4j topology** |
| `/api/v1/multi-origin-prefixes` | Neo4j |
| `POST /api/v1/admin/reload` | rebind the parquet views without a restart |

`/api/v1/analytics/hotspots` is the endpoint that justifies running both stores:
DuckDB's change log ranks prefixes by how much they moved and whether they are
still live, and Neo4j says who announces them and how well connected those
origins are. In the sample data it surfaces `84.205.80.0/24` — 14 changes, 7
withdrawals, `currently_live: false`, no origin left in the graph.

Nothing hard-codes a prefix or ASN: `/api/v1/examples` feeds the demo script,
the smoke test and the UI, so all three work on any MRT sample.

## Notes

- **`data/` is superseded by `work/`** and no longer mounted. Safe to delete.
- **`../graph/graph-compose.yaml` is superseded by this compose file.** Both
  define a Neo4j on 7474/7687, so they cannot run at once — bring that one down
  (`docker compose -f ../graph/graph-compose.yaml down`) before `make up`.
- Prefix routes need gin's raw-path matching (`UseRawPath`), otherwise `%2F`
  decodes to a path separator and the router 404s before any handler runs. See
  `internal/httpapi/router.go`.
- DuckDB `LIST` columns (`as_path`, origin lists) must be scanned into `any` and
  converted — `to_json(...)` into a `string` fails at the driver. See
  `intList` in `internal/store/duckdb.go`.
- Neo4j holds no persistent truth here: stages 4 and 5 rebuild it from the
  parquet files with `MERGE`, so dropping the volume costs one `make pipeline`.
- The Neo4j healthcheck probes with `cypher-shell`, not `wget`. Port 7474 starts
  listening before the `neo4j` *database* is queryable, so an HTTP-only check
  reports healthy while the loader stages still die with
  `Neo.TransientError.General.DatabaseUnavailable`.
- `route-state/app/reconstruct.py` replays its batch inside one transaction.
  Without it DuckDB auto-commits (and WAL-flushes) every statement in the loop —
  100 events took 4m52s that way versus roughly ten seconds now, and any larger
  `MRT_LIMIT` was simply not viable.
- Both graph loaders now `CALL db.awaitIndexes(300)` after creating their
  constraints, and the AS loader retries `TransientError` batches. Without the
  await, a clean load races the constraint's background index population and
  dies with `Neo.TransientError.Transaction.DeadlockDetected` — a coin flip that
  only reproduces when the Neo4j volume is empty, i.e. the clean-demo path.
